mn105:2.3: Sunakkhatta’s troubles are recorded at D. Sutta 24 and M. Sutta 12.
mn105:5.11: When people come to him with foolish questions having ulterior motives, or come pretending to have final knowledge (Arahantship) or some other attainment they do not actually have, the Buddha does not proceed to teach as he had intended. This is possibly a warning to Sunakkhatta.
mn105:10.1: Āneñja, a term usually meaning all four formless attainments, but here referring to the fourth form-sphere jhāna and the first two formless-sphere states.
mn105:18.2: ‘The Ascetic’ here refers to the Buddha himself.
mn105:18.4: ‘He might conceive this though it is not really so’ (evaṁmānī assa atathaṁ samānaṁ): that is, he overestimates his own attainment.
mn105:19.5: Sa-upādisesa (‘with some trace remaining’) and its counterpart anupādisesa (‘with no trace remaining’, 24.5) are more usually applied to Nibbāna itself, the first describing an Arahant or Buddha still alive, the second referring to one who has passed away leaving no trace of the aggregates. Here they are applied instead to the removal of the poison in the simile.
mn105:28.2: Upadhi—acquisitions, or essentials of existence: according to Comy these are of four kinds: (1) the five aggregates, (2) sensual desire, (3) mental defilements, and (4) kamma (intentional action).
